dedupe_keys.name: adapting overhead line design temperature to rising temperatures in the uk western power distribution and ena

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study shows how UK network operators, led here by Western Power Distribution, serving 8 million customers over 55,500 square kilometres, adapted overhead line design to rising temperatures. Heat reduces the thermal rating of lines and makes them sag towards the ground, trees and structures; UK utilities estimated that carrying capacity could fall by 4 to 9 percent by the middle of the century, and UKCP09 projected summer warming of up to 4 degrees by 2080 under medium emissions. Using the Met Office EP2 study of climate impacts on the energy industry and the Energy Networks Association task group, options such as taller poles, conductors with hotter limits and low-sag conductors were compared; the cheapest was raising the minimum design temperature of new routes, which typically adds 0.5 m to wood poles. UK rules require lines up to 33 kV to stay at least 5.8 m above ground at their highest likely temperature, and wood poles last 40 to 60 years, so replacement cycles can adopt the new standard. The page, published in 2018 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML. Coverage is the United Kingdom. Caveats: capacity losses are utility estimates and implementation is ongoing. It illustrates heat derating and sag in line rating and climate adaptation studies. Related records: case_study-finland-elenia-underground-cabling covers storm and snow adaptation of lines.
name: Adapting overhead line design temperature to rising temperatures in the UK (Western Power Distribution and ENA)
outcomes: The most cost-effective measure found was to raise the minimum design temperature of new overhead line routes, typically making wood poles 0.5 m taller at as little as about 10 GBP per pole.
